headline: Melbourne northern suburbs offering value despite negative sentiment; client case study shows purchase at $580k valued at $750k within 12 months
reasoning: Melbourne property has suffered more than any other Australian market in recent years, creating widespread caution among investors. However, selective positioning in the right suburbs with strong fundamentals is generating significant upside. A client property acquired in the northern Melbourne pocket of McCullum approximately 12 months ago at $580,000 has since been valued at $750,000, illustrating that headline fear is masking pockets of strong performance.
quote: Yeah. So this is the other thing is that I think Melbourne's got a pretty bad rap over the last couple of years in terms of the property market. Obviously prices have been hammered probably in Victoria more than anywhere else. And so I think a lot of people are pretty cautious about where do they invest, and rightly so. You obviously want to like right now it's even more important to be investing in the right areas with the right fundamentals. But we've actually got clients who came to us probably about 12 months ago. We helped him acquire a property up in the northern pocket of of Melbourne called McCullum. And through all this nonsense that's gone in the market over the last couple of months, all the fear mongering and scare, you know, scariness that's going on, Our clients ended up getting a, they purchased at about 580. We got a valuation through at about $750,000.

headline: Bullish on Melbourne property despite bad press, citing northern suburbs upside and valuation gains; sees strong 5–15 year upside from current levels
reasoning: Dory Senior argues Melbourne has been unfairly punished and that disciplined stock selection within the city can still generate strong returns. A client case study shows a property purchased at ~$580,000 in Melbourne's northern pocket (McCullum) recently valued at ~$750,000, despite adverse market conditions. He believes the market narrative overstates price declines, noting that most falls are concentrated in the $2M+ luxury segment rather than everyday price brackets. Nationally, prices fell only 0.9% last month and remain above January 2026 levels. He views a 5–15 year horizon as favourable for Melbourne given persistent housing demand from both buyers and renters.
quote: I think Melbourne still has a a lot of upside from where it is right now. And getting back to full circle, I guess to the the supply, right, People are always going to need somewhere to live, whether they're buying or renting. ... most of the drops that we're seeing is not in the everyday price bracket for most people, right? It's normally in the two racks and the, you know, the multi $1,000,000 suburbs, right? And if you actually look at the fundamental, the actual numbers for last like last month, our property prices fell by I think 0.9% and we're still above where we were back in January earlier this year.

headline: SMSF lending ban wiping out 30–50% of pre-sale buyers, forcing builders to shelve or scrap projects and deepening the supply shortfall
reasoning: The government's changes to self-managed superannuation fund lending have eliminated a large cohort of pre-sale buyers. Charlie Kate Kramer cited expectations that around 30% of pre-sales would be wiped out because that segment was dominated by SMSF investors. Some builders and developers saw SMSF buyers comprising 40–50% of their pre-sale base. Without those buyers, projects cannot meet pre-sale thresholds required to secure construction financing, leading to shelved or scrapped projects and a further reduction in housing supply.
quote: Charlie Kate Kramer actually came out in August talking about the fact that that they're expecting probably about 30% of pre sales to be wiped out because that was that 30% was made up by SMSF investors, people using the self managed Superfund to buy property. And obviously since the government's made it impossible to borrow money to do that through a self managed Superfund, not too many people are going to be going out there and have the appetite to pay for a property entirely in cash through their fund. So that completely wipes out people that are borrowing and I'm hearing some builders and developers that were a lot of their pre sales were made up by, you know, maybe 40 to even sometimes 50% of those type of buyers. So when you take those people out of the market, well, it doesn't magically mean that you know those sales are going to come from somewhere else.

headline: HIA flagging 4,000–5,000 houses likely scrapped from current market pipeline, adding to supply pressure
reasoning: The Housing Industry Association (HIA) has already indicated it expects at least 4,000 to 5,000 houses from the current pipeline to be scrapped, a meaningful deterioration in an environment already struggling with inadequate supply. This compounds the completions gap highlighted by the approval-versus-completion data.
quote: The HR coming out and talking about the fact that they've already seen in their space. I think it was about they're, they're expecting at least 4 to 5000 houses to be scrapped from the current crop in the in the market, which is obviously not a good, not a good environment for a market with which is already struggling with supply.

headline: SMSF investors displaced from residential are rotating into commercial property, representing lost residential supply capacity
reasoning: Following the effective ban on SMSF borrowing for residential property, investors are pivoting toward commercial real estate as an alternative avenue for SMSF capital deployment. While this supports commercial property demand, it permanently removes a source of funding for residential pre-sales and construction, further constraining housing supply with no offsetting gain on the residential side.
quote: Yeah, that's that's one of the big things that we've seen even in the last couple of months is obviously since the government has made it impossible for people to buy residential property through a self managed Superfund with lending, we're already starting to see people that have sort of shifted their approach and looking at other avenues and commercials definitely one of those big ones as well. So we're going to be losing, losing people that would have been investing in the residential market and helping with supply that'll ultimately end up going into commercial entirely.

headline: Rent-vesting increasingly viable path to wealth accumulation for first-home buyers priced out of owner-occupier market; housing affordability structurally difficult long-term
reasoning: Dory Senior believes getting into the housing market as an owner-occupier will not get easier over time, but cautions that some prospective buyers may be unnecessarily ruling themselves out. He advocates rent-vesting — continuing to rent in a desired lifestyle location while investing in investment properties elsewhere — as an effective alternative strategy. In his case study, a young couple who believed they could never afford to buy are now building a property portfolio to eventually fund an owner-occupied purchase. He frames the key differentiator as obtaining proper financial advice rather than accepting conventional wisdom.
quote: I think it's probably not going to get any easier. That's, that's, that's pretty clear in terms of getting into the market. Although I do also think that there's a certain cohort of people that are probably ruling themselves out of getting into being able to buy their own home. ... instead what they've done is they've gone down the rent vesting path. So instead of buying in a place to live for their first time, they've actually continued to rent where they want to live. They get the lifestyle and all that sort of stuff. And they get to it's a lot more affordable to rent while also putting the money to work and invest. And then their properties are going to ultimately help them down the line to be able to get into a home to, to live in for themselves.

headline: Completions at fourth-lowest 12-month rolling average since December 2014 despite rising approvals; rate hike expectations further undermine build confidence
reasoning: Despite approval numbers rising for roughly 12 months to around 206,000, actual completions sit at approximately 173,000 — a persistent structural gap. The most recent 12-month rolling average for completions is the fourth lowest since December 2014. An expected near-term RBA rate hike will further erode borrower confidence to build, compounding an already supply-constrained market.
quote: So this is the thing that the government loves to go on about is approval numbers and to to their credit they have been on the rise for probably the last 12 or so months. But when you actually look under underneath approvals, the thing that really matters ultimately is completions. And I think I was looking at the stats earlier, our most recent data looks at March for completions and the 12 month rolling average. That is the fourth lowest 12 month rolling average for completions that we've had since December of 2014.
